pages.title: The Blue Planet: Oceans & Running Water
bulletPoints: Over seventy percent of our planet Earth is covered in sparkling blue water.
Saltwater vs Freshwater: Over 97% of water is salty ocean; only 3% is fresh drinking water.
Water exists in three states: Liquid water in rivers, Solid ice in glaciers, and Gas vapor in clouds.
Observation: Trace on a world map how rivers flow from mountain peaks into the ocean.

pages.title: The Source: Where Rivers Are Born
bulletPoints: Mountain springs: Rain and melted snow seep through rocky cracks and bubble out as crystal-clear springs.
Glacial meltwater: Giant icy blue mountain glaciers slowly melt under summer sunshine to feed rivers.
Headwaters: High in the cool misty peaks, tiny bubbling brooks trickle over mossy pebbles.
The Continental Divide: The high mountain ridges that decide which ocean a river flows toward.

pages.title: Mountain Streams & Rushing Rapids
bulletPoints: V-shaped valleys: Fast rushing mountain water carves steep, narrow V-shaped gorges into hard stone.
Rapids: Rushing water tumbles violently over submerged boulders and churning white foam.
Erosion power: Tumbling stones bang against each other, grinding sharp rocks into smooth rounded pebbles.
Mountain wildlife: Spotted trout leap upstream against swift cold currents to lay their eggs.

pages.title: Waterfalls: Cascades & Giant Plunge Pools
bulletPoints: How waterfalls form: A river flows from hard rock over a softer rock layer that erodes away faster.
Plunge pools: Tons of crashing falling water carve deep circular churning pools at the base of the falls.
Angel Falls in Venezuela: The tallest uninterrupted waterfall on Earth, dropping nearly 1,000 meters!
Niagara Falls: Horseshoe-shaped roaring falls powering giant hydro-electric clean energy turbines.

pages.title: The Middle Course: Meanders & Wide Valleys
bulletPoints: As the river leaves the steep mountains, the land flattens and water slows down into gentle loops.
Meanders: S-shaped curves formed because water flows faster on the outer bank and slower on the inner bank.
Oxbow lakes: When a sharp meander loop gets cut off during a heavy flood, leaving a crescent-shaped lake.
Riverbanks: Lined with willow trees, tall cattails, and cozy nesting holes for river otters and kingfishers.

pages.title: Floodplains & Rich River Soil
bulletPoints: Floodplains: Flat, wide fertile land bordering a river that receives nutrient-rich mud during floods.
Alluvium / Silt: Mineral-rich sediment deposited by seasonal floods that creates the world's best farming soil.
Ancient civilizations: Egypt along the Nile, Mesopotamia along the Tigris and Euphrates, Indus Valley along the Indus.
Natural levees: Ridges of sand and sediment deposited right along river edges during high water.

pages.title: River Deltas: The Fan of Life
bulletPoints: Reaching the ocean: As a river meets the sea, it slows down completely and drops its heavy sediment load.
Distributaries: The main river branches out into dozens of smaller winding channels across a flat plain.
Delta shape: Often shaped like a giant triangle or Greek letter Delta (Δ) spreading into the sea.
Sundarbans Delta: The largest mangrove delta on Earth, home to Bengal tigers and dancing river dolphins.

pages.title: Estuaries: Where Saltwater Meets Fresh
bulletPoints: Estuary: A protected coastal bay where fresh river water mixes with salty ocean tides (brackish water).
Nurseries of the sea: Baby crabs, oysters, shrimp, and flounder grow up safe from big ocean predators here.
Tidal pulses: Twice each day, salty ocean tides surge up the estuary and then gently drain back out.
Salt marshes: Dense grasses filter coastal pollutants and protect shorelines from hurricane storm surges.

pages.title: Lakes: Inland Bowls of Fresh Water
bulletPoints: Freshwater lakes: Quiet inland bodies of water formed in glacial basins, volcanic craters, or tectonic rifts.
Lake Baikal in Siberia: The deepest and oldest freshwater lake on Earth, holding 20% of all unfrozen surface freshwater!
Crater Lake in Oregon: A breathtaking deep sapphire blue lake formed inside a collapsed ancient volcano caldera.
Oxidation and light: Clear sunlit shallows where floating water lilies bloom and dragonflies skim the surface.

pages.title: The Global Water Cycle: Endless Journey
bulletPoints: The water you drink today may have once quenched the thirst of a roaring Tyrannosaurus Rex millions of years ago!
Evaporation: Sunshine lifts water vapor high from oceans and lakes into the sky.
Condensation: Cloud formation in cool air layers.
Precipitation & Infiltration: Rain falls, soaks into the soil, refills aquifers, and flows back to the sea.

pages.title: Groundwater: The Hidden Underworld
bulletPoints: Aquifers: Underground layers of porous rock, gravel, and sand filled with cool, filtered fresh water.
The Water Table: The underground boundary level below which rocks and soil are completely saturated with water.
Natural springs: Places where underground water pressure pushes cool mineral water up to the surface.
Artesian wells: Deep wells drilled into confined aquifers where water gushes up naturally without pumps.

pages.title: Limestone Caves & Underground Rivers
bulletPoints: Karst topography: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide, becoming slightly acidic, and dissolves soft limestone rock.
Subterranean caverns: Vast underground cathedral chambers carved by ancient rushing underground rivers.
Stalactites: Icicle-like mineral stone spikes hanging down tightly from cave ceilings.
Stalagmites: Stone mounds built from mineral water drops splashing and evaporating on cave floors.

pages.title: Wetlands, Swamps & Marshes: Nature's Sponges
bulletPoints: Wetlands are land areas saturated with standing water for all or part of the year.
Nature's water filters: Wetland plant roots trap pollutants, heavy metals, and sediment, purifying dirty water.
Flood sponges: Absorbing massive surges of floodwater like a giant kitchen sponge, preventing city floods.
Biodiversity hot spots: Nesting grounds for migrating herons, cranes, turtles, and colorful dragonflies.

pages.title: The Mighty Oceans: Five Great Waters
bulletPoints: The Pacific Ocean: The largest and deepest ocean on Earth, covering more area than all land continents combined!
The Atlantic Ocean: S-shaped ocean separating the Americas from Europe and Africa.
The Indian Ocean: Warm tropical ocean bounded by Asia, Africa, and Australia with rich monsoon currents.
The Southern and Arctic Oceans: Icy polar seas covered with drifting pack ice and majestic white glaciers.

pages.title: Ocean Trenches & The Mariana Deep
bulletPoints: Challenger Deep: Located in the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, plunging nearly 11,000 meters down!
Crushing pressure: At the bottom of the trench, water pressure is over 1,000 times greater than at sea level.
Hydrothermal vents / Black smokers: Superheated mineral-rich water spewing from volcanic cracks on the seafloor.
Chemosynthesis: Deep-sea tubeworms and ghost crabs living completely without sunlight using sulfur chemicals.

pages.title: Tides: The Gravitational Dance
bulletPoints: Ocean tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun pulling on Earth's ocean water.
High tide: Ocean water bulges toward the moon, rising high onto sandy beaches twice every day.
Low tide: Water recedes into the sea, revealing tide pools full of colorful starfish and hermit crabs.
Spring tides: Occur during Full and New Moons when Sun, Moon, and Earth align, creating the highest tides.

pages.title: Ocean Currents: The Planetary Conveyor Belt
bulletPoints: Global conveyor belt: Giant rivers of moving water flowing inside the oceans driven by wind, salt, and temperature.
The Gulf Stream: Carries warm tropical Caribbean water across the Atlantic, keeping Western Europe pleasantly mild.
Cold deep currents: Cold, salty, dense water sinks near the North Pole and travels along the deep ocean floor.
Thermohaline circulation: Taking over 1,000 years for a single drop of water to complete one worldwide global loop!

pages.title: Coral Reefs: Rainforests of the Ocean
bulletPoints: Coral polyps: Tiny soft-bodied animals that build protective calcium carbonate limestone rock skeletons.
Zooxanthellae: Tiny algae living inside coral tissue that make food through photosynthesis and give corals bright colors.
The Great Barrier Reef in Australia: Stretches over 2,300 kilometers, visible even from orbiting space stations!
Home to marine life: Providing food and shelter for clownfish, sea turtles, moray eels, and graceful reef sharks.

pages.title: Human Connections: Rivers as Lifelines
bulletPoints: Drinking water: Fresh rivers and reservoirs supply fresh clean tap water for billions of families.
Hydroelectric energy: Giant clean dams convert the kinetic energy of falling water into clean electricity.
Trade and transportation: Barges and container ships navigate deep river channels to transport wheat and goods.
Recreation and peace: Kayaking through white-water canyons, fishing at sunrise, and listening to splashing waves.

pages.title: Cherishing & Protecting Our Waterways
bulletPoints: Clean water is a precious treasure: Less than one percent of all water on Earth is available for human use.
The problem of plastic: Millions of plastic bottles and straws pollute rivers and harm marine turtles.
River clean-up heroes: Planting trees along riverbanks to prevent soil erosion and picking up shoreline litter.
Our daily water promise: Turn off the tap while brushing teeth, take shorter showers, and cherish every single drop!
